The YOGI and DNP epicentral distances are 22.5 km and 500 km. The crust is 30 km deep above faster mantle. Ignore Earth curvature. Part C studies a tsunami generated by ocean-floor uplift, with density \(\rho\) and local ocean depth \(d\).

statement.text:
Earthquake, Volcano and Tsunami
Part A models the 2010 Merapi eruption as instantaneous, constant-volume mixing of magma mass \(m_m\) at \(T_m\) and water mass \(m_w\) at \(T_w\), followed by expansion. Neglect latent heats. Specific constant-volume heat capacities are \(c_{Vm},c_{Vw}\). Part B studies the 2006 Yogyakarta earthquake, origin time 22:54:00 UTC and hypocentre 15 km deep. The YOGI and DNP epicentral distances are 22.5 km and 500 km. The crust is 30 km deep above faster mantle. Ignore Earth curvature. Part C studies a tsunami generated by ocean-floor uplift, with density \(\rho\) and local ocean depth \(d\).
A.1. Mixture equilibrium temperature
Find the temperature after the first, constant-volume mixing stage.
A.2. Mixture equilibrium pressure
Model the mixture as ideal gas with molar volume \(v_e\). Find its equilibrium pressure.
A.3. Eruption velocity scaling
Find the gas-eruption velocity in terms of pressure \(p\), total mass \(m\), volume \(V\), and an unknown dimensionless factor \(K\).
B.1. Crust P-wave velocity

Read the P-wave arrival at YOGI from the seismogram and determine crust speed.
B.2. Direct and reflected arrivals
Find DNP travel times for the direct crustal ray and the ray reflected at the crust-mantle boundary.
B.3. Mantle velocity

The earliest DNP arrival is about 22:55:15. Use a critically refracted head wave along the boundary to find mantle speed.
B.4. Continuously varying crust
Approximate the source at the surface and let \(v(z)=v_0+az\), \(a>0\). The ray parameter is \(p=\sin\theta(z)/v(z)\), with angle from the vertical. Find epicentral distance X.
B.5. Travel-time integral
Express the travel time as an integral over depth.
B.6. Three-layer travel time

Approximate the integral with three layers: \(v_1=6.65,v_2=6.97,v_3=6.99\,\mathrm{km/s}\), \(p=0.143\,\mathrm{s/km}\), and thicknesses \(\delta z_1=6,\delta z_2=9,\delta z_3=15\,\mathrm{km}\).
C.1. Uplift potential energy

A raised water box has area \(\lambda L/2\), with \(L\gg\lambda\), and height \(h\). Find its gravitational energy above the original ocean surface.
C.2. Shallow-water wave speed
Use energy and mass conservation to obtain tsunami speed up to a dimensionless factor.
C.3. Shoaling amplitude
The depth changes slowly. At depth \(d_0\), amplitude is \(A_0\). Use energy conservation to find amplitude \(A(d)\).

children.text: Conservation of internal energy gives \(m_wc_{Vw}(T_e-T_w)+m_mc_{Vm}(T_e-T_m)=0\), hence \[T_e=\frac{m_wc_{Vw}T_w+m_mc_{Vm}T_m}{m_wc_{Vw}+m_mc_{Vm}}.\]
The ideal-gas law gives \(p_e=RT_e/v_e\), with universal gas constant R.
Pressure times volume is energy. Dimensional balance therefore requires \(u=K\sqrt{pV/m}\).

The path is \(\sqrt{22.5^2+15^2}=27.04\,\mathrm{km}\). The first arrival is about 4.7 s after origin, giving \(v_c\simeq5.75\,\mathrm{km/s}\). Arrival picks around 4.5 to 5.5 s give roughly 4.9 to 6.0 km/s.

The direct distance is \(\sqrt{500^2+15^2}=500.225\,\mathrm{km}\). Reflect the source in the boundary to obtain reflected distance \(\sqrt{500^2+45^2}=502.021\,\mathrm{km}\). Divide by the same crust speed. At 5.75 km/s the times are 87.00 s and 87.31 s, respectively. Small differences from published rounded times reflect the graph-derived crust speed.

The crustal vertical travel totals \(2\times30-15=45\,\mathrm{km}\). If \(\sin i=v_c/v_m\), the time is \[75=500/v_m+45\sqrt{v_c^{-2}-v_m^{-2}}.\] Solve with \(v_m>v_c\), obtaining approximately \(v_m=7.1\,\mathrm{km/s}\).
The turning depth obeys \(p(v_0+az_t)=1\). Along a ray \(dx/dz=pv/\sqrt{1-p^2v^2}\). Thus \[X=2\int_0^{z_t}\frac{p(v_0+az)}{\sqrt{1-p^2(v_0+az)^2}}dz=\frac2{ap}\sqrt{1-p^2v_0^2}.\]
Use \(dt=ds/v\), \(ds=dz/\cos\theta\): \[T(p)=2\int_0^{z_t}\frac{dz}{v(z)\sqrt{1-p^2v(z)^2}}.\] With slowness \(u=1/v\), the integrand is \(u^2/\sqrt{u^2-p^2}\).

Calculate \[T=2\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{\delta z_i}{v_i\sqrt{1-p^2v_i^2}}.\] Direct evaluation of the supplied speeds gives about 184.1 s. The source first rounds the slownesses to 0.1504, 0.1435 and 0.1431 s/km and obtains 151.64 s. Near the turning point the cancellation makes early rounding significant. Both conventions must be explained rather than treating the source figure as uniquely precise.
The raised mass is \(\rho\lambda Lh/2\), with centre at height \(h/2\). Hence \(E_p=\rho g\lambda Lh^2/4\).

Mass continuity gives horizontal water speed \(U\sim hv/d\). Equate potential energy \(\sim\rho g\lambda Lh^2\) and kinetic energy \(\sim\rho d\lambda LU^2\). The result is \(v\sim\sqrt{gd}\), the shallow-water speed.

Energy per horizontal area scales as \(A^2\). Conservation of energy flux gives \(A^2\sqrt{gd}=A_0^2\sqrt{gd_0}\), and therefore \[A=A_0(d_0/d)^{1/4}.\] This assumes no dissipation, reflection, breaking or lateral focusing.

solution.text:
Earthquake, Volcano and Tsunami
A.1. Mixture equilibrium temperature
Conservation of internal energy gives \(m_wc_{Vw}(T_e-T_w)+m_mc_{Vm}(T_e-T_m)=0\), hence \[T_e=\frac{m_wc_{Vw}T_w+m_mc_{Vm}T_m}{m_wc_{Vw}+m_mc_{Vm}}.\]
A.2. Mixture equilibrium pressure
The ideal-gas law gives \(p_e=RT_e/v_e\), with universal gas constant R.
A.3. Eruption velocity scaling
Pressure times volume is energy. Dimensional balance therefore requires \(u=K\sqrt{pV/m}\).
B.1. Crust P-wave velocity
The path is \(\sqrt{22.5^2+15^2}=27.04\,\mathrm{km}\). The first arrival is about 4.7 s after origin, giving \(v_c\simeq5.75\,\mathrm{km/s}\). Arrival picks around 4.5 to 5.5 s give roughly 4.9 to 6.0 km/s.
B.2. Direct and reflected arrivals
The direct distance is \(\sqrt{500^2+15^2}=500.225\,\mathrm{km}\). Reflect the source in the boundary to obtain reflected distance \(\sqrt{500^2+45^2}=502.021\,\mathrm{km}\). Divide by the same crust speed. At 5.75 km/s the times are 87.00 s and 87.31 s, respectively. Small differences from published rounded times reflect the graph-derived crust speed.
B.3. Mantle velocity
The crustal vertical travel totals \(2\times30-15=45\,\mathrm{km}\). If \(\sin i=v_c/v_m\), the time is \[75=500/v_m+45\sqrt{v_c^{-2}-v_m^{-2}}.\] Solve with \(v_m>v_c\), obtaining approximately \(v_m=7.1\,\mathrm{km/s}\).
B.4. Continuously varying crust
The turning depth obeys \(p(v_0+az_t)=1\). Along a ray \(dx/dz=pv/\sqrt{1-p^2v^2}\). Thus \[X=2\int_0^{z_t}\frac{p(v_0+az)}{\sqrt{1-p^2(v_0+az)^2}}dz=\frac2{ap}\sqrt{1-p^2v_0^2}.\]
B.5. Travel-time integral
Use \(dt=ds/v\), \(ds=dz/\cos\theta\): \[T(p)=2\int_0^{z_t}\frac{dz}{v(z)\sqrt{1-p^2v(z)^2}}.\] With slowness \(u=1/v\), the integrand is \(u^2/\sqrt{u^2-p^2}\).
B.6. Three-layer travel time
Calculate \[T=2\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{\delta z_i}{v_i\sqrt{1-p^2v_i^2}}.\] Direct evaluation of the supplied speeds gives about 184.1 s. The source first rounds the slownesses to 0.1504, 0.1435 and 0.1431 s/km and obtains 151.64 s. Near the turning point the cancellation makes early rounding significant. Both conventions must be explained rather than treating the source figure as uniquely precise.
C.1. Uplift potential energy
The raised mass is \(\rho\lambda Lh/2\), with centre at height \(h/2\). Hence \(E_p=\rho g\lambda Lh^2/4\).
C.2. Shallow-water wave speed
Mass continuity gives horizontal water speed \(U\sim hv/d\). Equate potential energy \(\sim\rho g\lambda Lh^2\) and kinetic energy \(\sim\rho d\lambda LU^2\). The result is \(v\sim\sqrt{gd}\), the shallow-water speed.
C.3. Shoaling amplitude
Energy per horizontal area scales as \(A^2\). Conservation of energy flux gives \(A^2\sqrt{gd}=A_0^2\sqrt{gd_0}\), and therefore \[A=A_0(d_0/d)^{1/4}.\] This assumes no dissipation, reflection, breaking or lateral focusing.
